idiom_name: hand-written binder struct plus wrapper function (context pointer)
implementation_notes: C has no closures, so a specialisation must be assembled from the pieces the language does have: a struct that holds the bound values and a wrapper function with the signature the consumer expects, which casts the context pointer back to that struct. The language's own substitute for the classic structure is the context parameter that callback APIs already thread through for you - glibc's qsort_r passes a void *arg to the comparator, pthread_create passes one void * to the thread routine, and cppreference presents these void* callbacks as the standard generic-interface pattern. That covers the dominant case (bind now, call through a framework later); a stored, reusable specialisation still needs a heap-allocated binder plus an explicit release, which is why hand-rolled generic curry machinery (void* argument arrays, preprocessor-generated wrappers, libffi trampolines) belongs to FFI and callback-table infrastructure rather than application code.
pitfalls: A binder that stores a pointer to a stack object (or to a temporary) produces the classic use-after-scope bug: qsort_r only borrows arg for the duration of the call, while a registered callback that keeps it must own a heap copy.

Nothing type-checks the wrapper: casting a void* context back to the wrong struct type, or passing a function pointer with a mismatched signature to a library, is undefined behaviour that the compiler cannot diagnose.
Without a garbage collector every heap-allocated binder needs an owner and an explicit free; registering the same binder in several places turns that into reference counting by hand.
